content:
Muslims are often asked a pointed question. If the Quran itself says that Jesus (peace be upon him) was born without a father, how can it deny that he is divine? Don Stewart of Blue Letter Bible states the Christian side plainly: "If Joseph were His true father, then Jesus would be only a human being."[1]

The Quran does affirm the virgin birth, in more than one surah and in plain words. It also tells the reader what the birth means, in the same passages.

This article aims to provide context to the question, insha'Allah, in five answers from the Quran, set beside what Christian theologians themselves say about the birth. The Quran's answer is one verse: "The similitude of Jesus before Allah is as that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him: 'Be'. And he was" (3:59).[2]

Stewart's argument is that a human father would have made Jesus "only a human being". Other Christians answer him from within their own faith.

An editorial in Christianity Today put it in one line: "The deity of Jesus Christ, of course, does not rest upon his virgin birth. Christians believe in the deity of Christ for quite different reasons."[3] Oliver Crisp, a Reformed theologian, defends the virgin birth as "fitting" for the incarnation, which is a claim about what suits it, short of a proof.[4]

So the claim that the birth proves divinity is a popular argument, and Christian writers of standing do not rest the doctrine on it. The Quran answers it all the same, and directly.

When the angels give Mary the news of a son, she asks: "O my Lord! How shall I have a son when no man hath touched me?" The answer is: "Even so: Allah createth what He willeth: When He hath decreed a plan, He but saith to it, 'Be,' and it is!" (3:47).[2]

Her question is about how a child can come without a father, and the answer is about God's power to create. Nothing in the verse gives the child a share in his Creator. We set out the title given to him in that annunciation, "a Word from Him", in our article on Jesus as a Word from God.

The Quran answers the argument from the fatherless birth by pointing to Adam (3:59). Al-Ṭabarī explains the comparison: God's creation of Jesus without a father is no more wondrous than His creation of Adam without father or mother, and the verse was revealed as an answer to the Christian delegation from Najran.[5]

The Bible makes the same comparison without meaning to. Luke's genealogy of Jesus ends: "the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God" (Luke 3:38).[6] If a birth without a human father made a son of God divine, Adam would have the stronger claim, and no Christian makes it for him. We set out the other sons of God in the Bible in sons of God in the Bible.

Surah Maryam tells the birth at length, and then gives Jesus his own first words: "I am indeed a servant of Allah: He hath given me revelation and made me a prophet" (19:30). Five verses later the surah gives the meaning: "It is not befitting to (the majesty of) Allah that He should beget a son. Glory be to Him! when He determines a matter, He only says to it, 'Be', and it is" (19:35).[2]

The miracle and the servanthood stand in one passage. We set out the whole account in our article on the birth of Jesus in Surah Maryam.

"And (remember) her who guarded her chastity: We breathed into her of Our spirit, and We made her and her son a sign for all peoples" (21:91). The same words are said of Mary in 66:12.[2]

Ibn Kathīr places the verse after the birth of John to an old man and a barren wife, and calls the birth of Jesus "even more wondrous", since "a child was born from a female without (the involvement of) a male".[7] The sign is of God's power, and Mary is part of it. The breath of God's spirit that made Jesus is the breath the Quran says God breathed into Adam (15:29).[2]

Matthew says Mary "was found pregnant by the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 1:18), and Luke has the angel say: "The Holy Spirit will come on you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you" (Luke 1:35).[6] Both describe God's power acting on Mary, which is the Quran's account as well.

Andrew Lincoln, a New Testament scholar, has examined how Matthew's account of the conception has been read and contested.[8] The divinity of Jesus, where Christians hold it, comes from other texts and from the creeds, chief among them "The Word became flesh" (John 1:14).[6]

The bottom line

The Quran affirms the virgin birth, and it affirms it as a sign of God's power. It answers the question of how with the command "Be", compares Jesus to Adam, gives the infant's first words as "I am indeed a servant of Allah", and joins Mary to her son as one sign. A Christian editorial says plainly that his deity does not rest on the birth.

The argument from the fatherless birth proves too much, since Adam had no father and no mother, and Luke himself calls him the son of God. The Quran's verdict stands in the surah that tells the story: "It is not befitting to (the majesty of) Allah that He should beget a son" (19:35).[2] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Don Stewart, "Why Is the Doctrine of the Virgin Birth Important?", in What Everyone Needs to Know about Jesus, Blue Letter Bible.
  2. Quran 3:45 to 47; 3:59; 19:16 to 35; 21:91; 66:12; 15:29, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. "Virgin-Born Rabbits", editorial, Christianity Today, 14 December 1984.
  4. Oliver D. Crisp, "On the 'Fittingness' of the Virgin Birth", Heythrop Journal 49, no. 2 (2008), pp. 197–221.
  5. Al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, ed. Maḥmūd Muḥammad Shākir, vol. 6, pp. 468–469, on Quran 3:59.
  6. Luke 3:23 to 38; Matthew 1:18 to 25; Luke 1:26 to 38; John 1:14 (World English Bible).
  7. Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, on Quran 21:91, abridged English translation on quran.com.
  8. Andrew T. Lincoln, "Contested Paternity and Contested Readings: Jesus' Conception in Matthew 1.18–25", Journal for the Study of the New Testament 34, no. 3 (2012), pp. 211–231.
